---
**The Usefulness of Getting Lost: Notes on Walking, Reading, and Paying Attention**

I have always been bad at arriving on time, not because I am disorganized in the ordinary way — I own a calendar, I set alarms, I pack the night before — but because I have a habit of noticing things on the way. A conversation overheard at a bus stop. A door left ajar in a side street I have walked down a hundred times. A used bookstore with a hand-painted sign that was not there last Tuesday. I will stop. I will look. I will, more often than I care to admit, follow a small curiosity down a side road that leads absolutely nowhere useful and be late, slightly bewildered, and strangely more awake for having done it.

For a long time I thought this was a defect. School taught me that efficiency was a virtue and wandering was its opposite. There were timetables to keep, essays to structure in five paragraphs, routes to optimize. I was taught to treat time like a corridor: narrow, straight, with doors only at the end. If you lingered you were wasting it. I believed that, more or less, until I began to suspect that the corridor model of a life was missing something essential — not just the decoration, but the point.

Getting lost, in the practical sense of taking a wrong turn, is usually an inconvenience. Getting lost in the larger sense — of being unmoored from a plan, a purpose, a tidy narrative about who you are supposed to become — can feel like a failure. And yet I have come to think that the times I have learned the most, felt the most alive, and understood the most about the places and people around me were not the times I followed directions perfectly. They were the times I paused, detoured, read the plaque on the wall though I did not need to, asked the question that had no immediate application, bought the book about a subject I knew I would never master.

This is an essay in praise of that pause. Not as a productivity hack — though it has, paradoxically, made me more productive in the long run — but as a way of living. It is about walking without needing to get anywhere, about libraries as quiet secular temples, about night trains and strangers and useless knowledge. It is about attention as a form of care.

### 1. The Map Is Not the Territory, and That Is Good News

A map is a beautiful lie. It flattens hills into lines, reduces a noisy street market to a perfect grid, turns a ten-minute climb in rain into an inch on paper. We need maps. Without them we would never leave our neighborhoods, never plan the trip, never teach a child how the river bends. But we mistake the map for the place at our peril, because the place always exceeds it.

I learned this in Lisbon, in a part of the city called Alfama, where the streets were laid down long before anyone thought about cars or urban planning, and every few meters the road narrows, steepens, turns back on itself like a sentence that has lost its thread and started again. I had a phone with a blue dot and a voice that said, "In 50 meters, turn left." I turned left and was in a dead end full of laundry and a cat asleep on a scooter. I turned right and was in a courtyard where an old man was mending a net and whistled at me without malice, the way you whistle at weather.

If I had stayed glued to the blue dot, I would have arrived at my destination twelve minutes sooner and remembered almost nothing. Because I got lost — properly, unhappily, wonderfully lost — I remember the smell of fried oil from a tasca, the blue tiles chipped to reveal the clay beneath, the way the light fell sideways through the hills. I remember the city not as a destination but as a texture.

Maps are answers. Walking around without one, or with one loosely in your pocket, is a question. Questions are slower and usually more interesting. A map tells you where to go. A detour tells you what is there.

There is a larger lesson in this. We have become a civilization that treats every experience as something to be navigated efficiently from start to finish. We skip the intro, we read the summary, we watch the highlights. We let algorithms draw straight lines between our interests, and we are surprised when our inner lives feel monochromatic. The territory — actual life, actual curiosity, actual thought — is messier and more fertile than any route directly to a goal. Leave room for the wrong turn. The wrong turn is where the cat is sleeping on the scooter.

### 2. Walking Is Thinking With Your Feet

I walk everywhere now, not out of principle but out of a slow realization that my brain works best when my legs are moving. I do not mean exercise in the optimized sense, though I am sure the endorphins help. I mean the old, shambling, stop-and-start kind of walking, the kind without podcasts or playlists, the kind where you notice the wood pigeon on the ledge and the way the clouds are arranging themselves like a slow argument about the weather.

Philosophers knew this. Aristotle walked with his students. Darwin had his sand walk. Beethoven wandered the Vienna Woods with manuscript paper sticking out of his pocket. Virginia Woolf said she could think clearly only when she was walking. I am not a genius, but I recognize the pattern in myself: a problem that looks impenetrable at my desk will, after two miles without trying to solve it, suddenly present its edges. Not the whole solution, but the shape of it. The feet untie something the mind was knotting.

Walking also restores a sense of scale. Everything on a screen is the same size: a war, a wedding, a recipe, a cat video. On foot, things insist on their actual proportions. A hill is a hill. You feel it in your calves. Distance becomes effort again, and effort becomes respect. You arrive at a place — a market, a hilltop, a friend's house — having earned it in the modest currency of your own body. It changes how you look at it.

And walking is democratic. You do not need special equipment. You do not need permission. You can be rich or poor, young or old, and the pavement is common ground. The great flâneurs of Paris wrote about this, but you do not need Paris. Any town has its back streets, its canal path, its slightly overgrown shortcut through the park that is not on the official map but is used by everyone who actually lives there. To walk a place is to begin to belong to it, in a small, unprovable way.

I have a favorite walk that starts at my front door and makes a loop that should take twenty minutes. It often takes an hour because I stop to watch the river. There is a heron who lives there, or perhaps a succession of herons who have agreed to be the same heron for the purposes of my story. He stands statue-still in water that moves and moves and does not seem to bother him at all. I have learned more about patience from that bird than from any book about mindfulness. He is not meditating. He is just being a heron. That is enough of a lesson.

### 3. Libraries and the Quiet Radicalism of Browsing

There is a particular pleasure that modern life has almost entirely removed: the pleasure of finding something you were not looking for, in a place that keeps everything. I feel it most strongly in libraries and secondhand bookshops, those wonderful, slightly chaotic archives of other people's attention.

A library is a radical place. It says: here are thousands of books, written by thousands of people, on subjects you did not know existed, and you may take any of them home for free. No one will sell you the one you “really” need. No algorithm will narrow your choices to five tasteful options based on your previous clicks. You have to wander the stacks. You have to let your eye catch on a Georgian poetry collection shelved between a manual on plumbing and a biography of a lighthouse keeper. You have to pull it out and read the first line, just to see.

Browsing is inefficient. It is also how I have discovered most of what I love. I went into a secondhand shop in Edinburgh looking for a specific novel and came out with a battered field guide to British fungi and a book of letters from a lighthouse keeper’s wife in 1892. I have never needed to identify a mushroom in the wild, and I will likely never live in a lighthouse, but those books rewired something in me. They reminded me that the world is wider than my current preoccupations.

Libraries teach a different kind of attention than the internet. On the internet, attention is extracted. In a library, attention is offered. The books sit there, patiently, not demanding to be liked, not updating themselves to keep you hooked. You choose. You commit to carrying a heavy volume home on the bus. You read it slowly because you know you have three weeks before you must return it. The deadline is not urgency but space: a small, humane pressure to make room.

I think we underestimate how much our inner lives depend on this kind of unoptimized encounter. We think we know what we want, but often what we want is only what we have already learned to want. The library shelf, with its indifference to our personal brand, corrects that. It suggests that curiosity does not have to be justified. You can be interested in the history of forks for an afternoon. You do not have to turn it into a career, a content vertical, a personality trait. You can just be curious, and then move on, and the curiosity will have done its work anyway.

### 4. Night Trains and the Art of Having Nowhere to Be

If walking is thinking with your feet, the night train is thinking with the whole landscape sliding past you while you do absolutely nothing that can be measured. I love night trains in a way that is disproportionate to their practical merits. They are slow. They are often uncomfortable. They smell of warm metal and someone else's dinner. And I would choose one over a smooth flight any day, given the choice.

On a night train, you surrender. You cannot check your position every five minutes. You cannot optimize your arrival. You hand over your vigilance to a driver you will never meet and a track you cannot see, and you lie in a bunk that is slightly too short and listen to the rhythm: clickety-clack, clickety-clack, a sound that has been putting people to sleep for over a century. The world outside is a dark blur; the world inside is a small, temporary community of snorers and readers and people who have taken off their shoes with great ceremony.

There is something profoundly restorative about being in transit at night, between places, belonging to neither. For a few hours, you are not required to be productive, or responsive, or anywhere in particular. Your phone, mercifully, has no signal. You watch the moon move across a field, you watch a single farmhouse light, you think about the people who live their whole lives in the places you are merely passing through. It induces a kind of humility. You are a story passing through other stories.

I once took a night train from Vienna to Venice that was delayed by snow, and we spent the better part of the morning almost motionless in the Alps, breath visible in the carriage, all of us strangers suddenly united in the mildly thrilling inconvenience. Someone produced a thermos. Someone else had biscuits. We talked about nothing in particular. When we finally arrived, hours late, no one was angry in the way people are angry at airports. We had been given time, unscheduled, and we had used it to be briefly, accidentally, human with each other.

We have designed most travel to eliminate that in-between. The in-between is where reflection lives. It is where the mind catches up with the body. A flight deposits you, jet-lagged, into a new place with your thoughts still back home. A night train lets your thoughts travel at the same speed as you.

### 5. Conversations With Strangers

One of the saddest losses of modern urban life is not crime or noise but the disappearance of the casual conversation with a stranger. We have trained ourselves to keep our heads down, our headphones in, our faces neutral. We do it for safety, for efficiency, for a desire not to be bothered. I understand all of that. And yet I miss the small, gratuitous kindnesses that used to interrupt a day: the person at the market who tells you how to pick a melon, the taxi driver who asks where you are from and then tells you, at length, about his brother in Canada.

I have made a practice of allowing those conversations. Not forcing them — you can always tell when someone does not want to talk, and respecting that is part of the practice — but receiving them. It is surprising how often a stranger will tell you something true, something they would not tell a friend. The barista who explains that her son just got into art school. The old man on the bench who knew my grandfather. The woman in the bookshop who, seeing me hesitate between two novels, says, “Take the sad one. The sad one is better.” She is right.

These micro-conversations are a form of education no course can replicate. They are local knowledge in its most human form. A guidebook will tell you the history of a neighborhood. A stranger will tell you which bakery still makes bread the old way and which one is run by his nephew and therefore diplomatically to be avoided on Saturdays. That knowledge is biased, partial, warm. It is better than accurate.

There is also something about being perceived, briefly and kindly, by someone who owes you nothing. For a few minutes, you are not your job title or your online profile. You are just a person at a bus stop in the rain. Someone says, “Cold one, eh?” and you are both, for a moment, in the same weather, literally and otherwise. It is a small thing, but small things are the mortar of a livable world.

### 6. The Joy of Useless Knowledge

Somewhere along the way, we decided that learning had to pay for itself. If you study something, it should lead to a skill, a job, a better version of yourself that can be measured. This is not entirely wrong — we have limited time, and practical knowledge matters. But it has produced a culture where curiosity feels selfish unless it can be monetized.

I am here to defend useless knowledge. Not as a rejection of usefulness, but as a reminder that the most useful things often begin as useless. The number theorist who played with prime numbers for fun laid the groundwork for cryptography that now secures every online transaction. The botanists pressing flowers in the 18th century gave us half of modern medicine. You cannot know in advance which curiosity will matter. And even if it never “matters” in that large sense, it matters in the small sense of making a life more interesting to live.

I collect useless facts the way other people collect train sets. I know that octopuses have three hearts and blue blood. I know that the first oranges were not orange but green. I know that the song “You Are My Sunshine” was once recorded as a warning about the dangers of excess sunshine. I know that there is a species of jellyfish that is biologically immortal, and another that is made almost entirely of water and light. None of this will help me fix a sink or get a promotion. All of it helps me feel that the world is stranger and more wonderful than my daily routine suggests.

Useless knowledge is a form of play. Play, for adults, has been made suspect: if it does not produce, it must be procrastination. But play is how children learn, and adults do not stop needing to learn. To follow a question because it is beautiful, not because it is profitable, is an act of intellectual freedom. It is also, I suspect, an act of resistance in a world that would prefer us to be consumers all the way down.

At worst, useless knowledge makes you good company at dinner. At best, it reorganizes your mind in ways you cannot predict. You go down a rabbit hole about medieval spices and come out understanding trade routes, colonialism, and why your curry tastes the way it does. The rabbit hole was the point. The lesson was smuggled in.

### 7. Attention as a Form of Care

All of these things — walking, browsing, riding, talking, wondering — come down to one simple, difficult practice: paying attention. Not in the frantic, multitasking way we usually mean it, but in the older sense of turning your mind toward something and letting it stay there for a while.

Attention is care. When you really listen to a friend, you are not waiting for your turn to speak. You are noticing the hesitation before the sentence, the joke that almost wasn’t a joke. When you really look at a tree, you are not cataloguing it for later use. You are noticing the way the light catches the new leaves and how the old branch has grown around a wire. The world becomes more itself when you look at it longer.

We live in an economy that competes for our attention and then sells us the feeling that we have none left. The genius of the phone is not that it is interesting — much of it is not — but that it fragments our attention into pieces too small to do anything with. We end the day tired but not satisfied, having seen everything and noticed nothing.

Practicing attention, then, is a quiet rebellion. It does not require a retreat or a new app. It requires returning. Returning to the page you were reading. Returning to the walk you are on. Returning to the person talking to you. The mind will wander — it is a mind — but you bring it back, gently, again and again. That returning is the exercise. It is how a garden is tended, a friendship is kept, a thought is developed.

I have found that attention grows the way a muscle grows: not by staring harder, but by practicing more often in low-stakes situations. Notice the weather. Notice the texture of your coffee mug. Notice the exact shade of the sky at 6:42 on a Tuesday. Over time, the noticing spreads. You start to notice people. You start to notice patterns. You start to notice what you do not know, which is the beginning of wisdom and the end of arrogance.

There is a Japanese word, *shizen*, often translated as “natural” or “spontaneous,” but it also means a kind of unforced state of being. A river is *shizen*. A person in *shizen* is not trying to be impressive. They are just fully present in what they are doing. I think attention is the path to *shizen*, not because it is effortless, but because effort, when it is loving, ceases to feel like effort.

### 8. Going Home the Long Way

I still have a calendar. I still try to be on time. I still use maps when I need to get somewhere quickly in an unfamiliar city, and I am grateful for them. The point is not to romanticize inefficiency or to pretend that detours are always delightful. Sometimes a wrong turn is just a wrong turn, and you are late and wet and annoyed, and the cat on the scooter is unimpressed.

The point is to leave room. To build a life with margins, like a well-designed page. Margins are not empty space; they are where notes are written, where the eye rests, where the binding can flex without tearing. A life without margins tears.

So I walk the long way home, sometimes. I browse the shelf I did not plan to browse. I take the night train when I could fly. I ask the question I know I “shouldn’t” ask because it might lead to a long answer. I follow the useless thread. Not always — often I am tired, or rushed, or in a bad mood, and I want the straight line. But I try to remember that the straight line is not the only line, and it is rarely the one I remember years later.

Years from now, I will not remember the exact time I arrived at the grocery store. I will remember the heron. I will remember the woman in the bookshop and the sad novel, which was indeed better. I will remember the snow in the Alps and the biscuits and the brief, accidental community of strangers. I will remember the fungi book I never needed and the lighthouse letters I never forgot.

That is, I suspect, what a good life looks like from the inside: not a series of optimized arrivals, but a series of attended moments, strung together by curiosity. We arrive, eventually, at home. But the best part is the long way there, and the willingness, along the way, to get a little lost — and to find, in the getting lost, exactly what we were looking for without knowing we were looking for it at all.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A polished, essayistic reflection uses personal anecdotes and recurring images to make its argument feel lived rather than merely abstract.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, observant, and gently self-deprecating: lateness and detours become openings to notice a cat, a heron, a stranger’s remark, or the texture of a place. Its pathos lies in resistance to a hurried, optimized life and in a longing for ordinary encounters that make people feel briefly connected. The essay invites the reader to loosen their grip on efficiency—not to abandon practical plans, but to leave room for curiosity, unmeasured time, and attention as a form of care.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds walking, libraries and secondhand bookshops, night trains, conversations with strangers, and apparently useless knowledge. These recurring scenes support a moral claim that attention and curiosity enrich life in ways that cannot be reduced to productivity. Maps, margins, detours, the heron, and the sleeping cat give the argument a consistent vocabulary of leaving room for what a plan cannot anticipate.

## Evidence line
> The wrong turn is where the cat is sleeping on the scooter.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a coherent, distinctive motif of detours and attention across many concrete scenes, while its polished public-facing structure also shapes the voice.
